    Glossary of terms and signs

    Words: 3781

    Two references in one place: how the signs of mathematical notation are read, and what each concept of the course means.

    Main idea of the page #

    A glossary is not for memorising but for coming back. Reading a block, you meet a concept introduced a few blocks earlier, and instead of leafing back you open its card right in the text or come here. Each entry says three things: what it is in one sentence, why it is built exactly so, and where in the course it first appeared. The entries stand in the order they appear in the course, not alphabetically: that way you see what grew out of what.

    The language of notation: how the signs are read #

    A sign you have seen a hundred times and never heard aloud lets you neither ask a question nor check yourself. So for each sign below it says how it is pronounced, not only what it means.

    • ±\pm plus or minus: two values at once, with a plus and with a minus. Block 4 · Equations and inequalities.
    • ≠\neq is not equal to: the numbers are different. Block 1 · Number and operations.
    • ≤\leq is less than or equal to: a non-strict inequality, the endpoint is included. Block 4 · Equations and inequalities.
    • |a||a| the absolute value of a: the distance from a to zero. Block 1 · Number and operations.
    • a\sqrt{a} the square root of a: the non-negative number whose square is a. Block 6 · Power, root, logarithm.
    • an\sqrt[n]{a} the n-th root of a: the number that gives a when raised to the power n. Block 6 · Power, root, logarithm.
    • ana^n a to the power n: the product of n factors a. Block 6 · Power, root, logarithm.
    • logab\log_a b the logarithm of b to base a: the exponent to which a is raised to get b. Block 6 · Power, root, logarithm.
    • ⟺\iff if and only if: equivalence, both statements are true or both are false. Block 4 · Equations and inequalities.
    • ⟹\implies implies: the right statement follows from the left one. Block 4 · Equations and inequalities.
    • ∈\in belongs to: an element is in a set. Block 1 · Number and operations.
    • ∪\cup union: the numbers that lie in at least one of the intervals. Block 4 · Equations and inequalities.
    • ∅\varnothing the empty set: there are no solutions. Block 4 · Equations and inequalities.
    • ∞\infty infinity: not a number; in an interval it always takes a round bracket. Block 1 · Number and operations.
    • f′(x)f'(x) f prime of x: the derivative of the function f. Block 8 · Derivative and integral.
    • ∫ab\int_a^b the integral from a to b: what has accumulated over the interval from a to b. Block 8 · Derivative and integral.
    • n!n! n factorial: the product of all natural numbers from 1 to n. Block 9 · Combinatorics, probability, statistics.
    • CnkC_n^k n choose k: the number of combinations of k out of n. Block 9 · Combinatorics, probability, statistics.
    • ∠A\angle A angle A: the angle with its vertex at the point A. Block 10 · Figures in the plane.
    • ⟂\perp is perpendicular to: lines or vectors at a right angle. Block 12 · Coordinates and vectors.
    • ∥\parallel is parallel to: the lines do not meet and lie in one plane. Block 10 · Figures in the plane.
    • π\pi pi: the ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter, about 3.14. Block 7 · Trigonometry.

    How the site is built: law, corollary, method #

    Corollary law ⟹ corollary #

    A theorem derived from a law in a few lines and resting on it.

    On a block page a corollary stands under its law in a frame «Corollary of the law …» with a short derivation. In the frequency of laws a corollary is counted for its law: it does not add a law.

    First met in: Landing page · How each page is built

    Method law + law #

    A scheme for combining several laws to solve a whole class of tasks.

    A method stands in the «Practice» step: a three-step scheme and a trainer task. A method is not a new law: each of its steps rests on a law of the site.

    First met in: Landing page · How each page is built

    1 · Number and operations #

    Rational number p/q #

    A number that can be written as a fraction p/q with an integer p and a natural q.

    Every rational number is a terminating or a recurring decimal, and the other way round: the recurring part disappears under subtraction, as in the worked example of the number 2.(3).

    First met in: Block 1 · Number and operations · Concept

    Irrational number √2, π #

    A real number that cannot be written as a common fraction.

    Its decimal expansion is infinite and non-recurring. Irrational numbers fill the «holes» between the rational ones on the number line.

    First met in: Block 1 · Number and operations · Concept

    Real numbers ℝ #

    All rational and irrational numbers together: every point of the number line.

    It is on the real numbers that all the laws of school algebra act; you can divide by any number except zero.

    First met in: Block 1 · Number and operations · Concept

    Absolute value |a| #

    The distance from a number to zero on the number line; an absolute value is never negative.

    So |a| = a for a ≥ 0 and |a| = −a for a < 0. The expression −a here is not negative: it is a itself that is negative.

    First met in: Block 1 · Number and operations · Concept

    Interval [a; b), (a; +∞) #

    All the numbers between two bounds; a square bracket includes the bound, a round one does not.

    Infinity is always written with a round bracket: it is not a number and cannot be reached.

    First met in: Block 1 · Number and operations · Concept

    Formulas of short multiplication (a ± b)², a² − b² #

    Ready-made expansions of products, each of them a consequence of the distributive law.

    You do not have to remember them: any of them can be derived by multiplying out the brackets in half a minute. In detail, in block 3.

    First met in: Block 1 · Number and operations · Why it is so

    Zero product ab = 0 #

    A product equals zero if and only if at least one factor equals zero.

    Solving equations by factorisation stands on this law. Both factors must be defined: a factor that makes no sense gives no root.

    First met in: Block 1 · Number and operations · Why it is so

    Divisibility test by 2, 3, 5, 9, 10 #

    A rule that shows whether a number is divisible without doing the division.

    For 3 and 9 you look at the sum of the digits, because 10 = 9 + 1; for 2, 5, 10 at the last digit, for 4 at the last two.

    First met in: Block 1 · Number and operations · Why it is so

    GCD and LCM GCD(a, b) · LCM(a, b) = ab #

    The greatest common divisor and the least common multiple of two natural numbers.

    The GCD takes each prime factor at its lowest power, the LCM at its highest.

    First met in: Block 1 · Number and operations · Why it is so

    2 · Ratio, proportion, percent #

    Percent 1 % = 1/100 #

    One hundredth part; a percentage is always taken of some whole.

    Without an answer to the question «of what» a percentage has no value: 20 % of 100 and 20 % of 120 are different numbers.

    First met in: Block 2 · Ratio, proportion, percent · Concept

    Whole, part, share A = B · p/100 #

    The whole is what you count from, the part is what was taken, the share is what fraction the part makes up.

    The law of the part links three quantities, and a percentage task asks about one of them.

    First met in: Block 2 · Ratio, proportion, percent · Concept

    Proportion a/b = c/d #

    An equality of two ratios; its basic property is ad = bc.

    Multiply both sides by bd, and the property becomes obvious.

    First met in: Block 2 · Ratio, proportion, percent · Why it is so

    Inverse proportion v · t = const #

    A dependence in which the product of two quantities is constant.

    Increasing one quantity k times decreases the other k times, but not by the same percentage: +50 % of speed gives −33⅓ % of time.

    First met in: Block 2 · Ratio, proportion, percent · Why it is so

    3 · Algebraic expressions #

    Identity always true #

    An equality that is true for all admissible values of the variables.

    An identity transformation changes the form of an expression but not its value.

    First met in: Block 3 · Algebraic expressions · Concept

    Polynomial sum of monomials #

    A sum of monomials, products of numbers and powers of variables.

    Polynomials are added, subtracted and multiplied by the laws of operations of block 1.

    First met in: Block 3 · Algebraic expressions · Concept

    Domain of admissible values (the domain) domain #

    The values of the variables for which an expression makes sense.

    The denominator is not zero, under an even root it is non-negative, under a logarithm it is positive. The domain is found before solving, not after.

    First met in: Block 3 · Algebraic expressions · Concept

    4 · Equations and inequalities #

    Completing the square (x + a)² + c #

    Transforming an expression so that the square of a sum or a difference appears in it.

    Hence the quadratic formula and the vertex of a parabola.

    First met in: Block 4 · Equations and inequalities · Why it is so

    Root of an equation f(x) = 0 #

    A value of the variable that turns the equation into a true numerical equality.

    Not to be confused with the n-th root: these are different concepts with the same name.

    First met in: Block 4 · Equations and inequalities · Concept

    Equivalent equations ⇔ #

    Equations with the same sets of roots.

    Solving is a chain of equivalent steps. Dividing by an expression with a variable and squaring can be non-equivalent.

    First met in: Block 4 · Equations and inequalities · Concept

    Extraneous root check #

    A number that appeared after a non-equivalent step and does not satisfy the original equation.

    After squaring, each root is checked by substitution.

    First met in: Block 4 · Equations and inequalities · Concept

    System of equations { … } #

    Several equations that must hold at the same time.

    A solution of a system is a common solution of all its equations; the methods are substitution and addition.

    First met in: Block 4 · Equations and inequalities · Concept

    Discriminant D = b² − 4ac #

    An expression whose sign shows how many real roots a quadratic equation has.

    Two roots for D > 0, one for D = 0, none for D < 0.

    First met in: Block 4 · Equations and inequalities · Why it is so

    Vieta's theorem x₁ + x₂ = −b/a #

    The sum and the product of the roots of a quadratic equation, expressed through its coefficients.

    First check the discriminant: the theorem speaks of roots that may not exist.

    First met in: Block 4 · Equations and inequalities · Why it is so

    Interval method signs between zeros #

    Solving inequalities by the signs of the factors on the intervals between their zeros.

    The zeros of the denominator are always punctured: the expression makes no sense there.

    First met in: Block 4 · Equations and inequalities · Laws

    5 · Function and sequence #

    Function y = f(x) #

    A rule that assigns exactly one number to each x of the domain of definition.

    A function describes a dependence as a whole; an equation only asks where it equals a certain number.

    First met in: Block 5 · Function and sequence · Concept

    Domain of definition D(f) #

    All values of the argument for which the function makes sense.

    It is found before anything else: both the graph and the roots depend on it.

    First met in: Block 5 · Function and sequence · Concept

    Even and odd function f(−x) = ±f(x) #

    A function whose graph is symmetric about the Oy axis (even) or about the origin (odd).

    Parity makes sense only on a symmetric domain of definition.

    First met in: Block 5 · Function and sequence · Concept

    Increasing and decreasing monotonicity #

    A function is increasing if a larger argument gives a larger value.

    Monotonicity is found from the sign of the derivative (block 8).

    First met in: Block 5 · Function and sequence · Concept

    Sequence aₙ #

    A function of a natural argument: each number n has its term of the sequence.

    So everything said about functions works for sequences too.

    First met in: Block 5 · Function and sequence · Concept

    Arithmetic progression aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1) #

    A sequence in which each term is greater than the previous one by the same number d.

    The sum of the first n terms is the mean of the first and the last, multiplied by n.

    First met in: Block 5 · Function and sequence · Concept

    Geometric progression bₙ = b₁qⁿ⁻¹ #

    A sequence in which each term is the same number q times the previous one.

    The sum formula does not work for q = 1: then all the terms are equal.

    First met in: Block 5 · Function and sequence · Concept

    Vertex of a parabola x₀ = −b/(2a) #

    The point of a parabola at which the function reaches its least or greatest value.

    It is found by completing the square.

    First met in: Block 5 · Function and sequence · Why it is so

    6 · Power, root, logarithm #

    Power aⁿ #

    The product of n equal factors a; fractional and negative exponents extend this definition.

    The equality aⁿ = b has three participants, and a question about each of them gives a power, a root or a logarithm.

    First met in: Block 6 · Power, root, logarithm · Concept

    n-th root ⁿ√b #

    The number that gives b when raised to the power n.

    An even root of a negative number does not exist among the real numbers; an odd one does.

    First met in: Block 6 · Power, root, logarithm · Concept

    Arithmetic root √a ≥ 0 #

    The non-negative number whose square equals a given non-negative number.

    That is exactly why √(a²) = |a|, not a.

    First met in: Block 6 · Power, root, logarithm · Why it is so

    Logarithm logₐ b #

    The exponent to which the base a must be raised to get b.

    It exists only for a > 0, a ≠ 1, b > 0. A logarithm turns multiplication into addition.

    First met in: Block 6 · Power, root, logarithm · Concept

    7 · Trigonometry #

    Radian 180° = π #

    The angle that stands on an arc as long as the radius.

    A full circle is 2π radians. In radians an angle becomes an ordinary number, and the trigonometric functions become functions of a number.

    First met in: Block 7 · Trigonometry · Concept

    Unit circle x² + y² = 1 #

    The circle of radius 1 centred at the origin, on which angles are measured off.

    Almost all the formulas of trigonometry are symmetries of this circle or Pythagoras' theorem on it.

    First met in: Block 7 · Trigonometry · Concept

    Sine and cosine sin α, cos α #

    The ordinate and the abscissa of the point of the unit circle that corresponds to the angle α.

    So both lie between −1 and 1.

    First met in: Block 7 · Trigonometry · Main idea

    Periodic function f(x + T) = f(x) #

    A function whose values repeat after a constant step, the period.

    Hence the infinite series of roots of trigonometric equations.

    First met in: Block 7 · Trigonometry · Concept

    Pythagoras' theorem c² = a² + b² #

    In a right triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the legs.

    Hence the distance between points, the equation of a circle, the basic trigonometric identity. Its generalisation to any triangle is the cosine rule.

    First met in: Block 7 · Trigonometry · Main idea

    8 · Derivative and integral #

    Derivative f′(x) #

    The instantaneous rate of change of a function; the gradient (US: slope) of the tangent to its graph.

    The sign of the derivative shows where the function increases and where it decreases.

    First met in: Block 8 · Derivative and integral · Concept

    Extremum point max, min #

    An interior point where the function goes from increasing to decreasing or the other way round.

    A zero of the derivative is only a candidate; the extremum is decided by a change of sign of the derivative.

    First met in: Block 8 · Derivative and integral · Concept

    Antiderivative F′ = f #

    A function whose derivative equals the given function.

    Two antiderivatives of one function differ by a constant.

    First met in: Block 8 · Derivative and integral · Concept

    Definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx #

    The quantity accumulated over an interval; for a non-negative function, the area under the graph.

    It is computed by the Newton - Leibniz formula: F(b) − F(a).

    First met in: Block 8 · Derivative and integral · Concept

    9 · Combinatorics, probability, statistics #

    Permutation Pₙ = n! #

    An ordering of all n elements.

    The product rule: n options for the first place, n − 1 for the second, and so on.

    First met in: Block 9 · Combinatorics, probability, statistics · Concept

    Arrangement Aₙᵏ #

    An ordered choice of k elements out of n.

    The order matters: a password, a queue, a distribution of places.

    First met in: Block 9 · Combinatorics, probability, statistics · Concept

    Combination Cₙᵏ #

    An unordered choice of k elements out of n.

    The order does not matter: a team, a committee, a set. So Cₙᵏ = Aₙᵏ / k!.

    First met in: Block 9 · Combinatorics, probability, statistics · Concept

    Equally likely outcomes none prevails #

    Outcomes of a trial none of which has an advantage over the others.

    Only among them does the classical probability m/n work.

    First met in: Block 9 · Combinatorics, probability, statistics · Concept

    Classical probability P(A) = m/n #

    The share of favourable outcomes among all the equally likely ones.

    A probability is always between 0 and 1; the probability of the opposite event is 1 − P(A).

    First met in: Block 9 · Combinatorics, probability, statistics · Main idea

    Median the middle by place #

    The value that stands in the middle of an ordered row of data.

    Unlike the mean, the median is not sensitive to one very large value.

    First met in: Block 9 · Combinatorics, probability, statistics · Concept

    10 · Figures in the plane #

    Transversal corresponding, alternate angles #

    A line that crosses two other lines and forms pairs of angles with them.

    The equality of these angles is both a test and a property of parallel lines.

    First met in: Block 10 · Figures in the plane · Concept

    Similar triangles k #

    Triangles of the same shape: the angles are equal, the sides are proportional.

    Two equal angles are enough. Trigonometry grew out of similarity.

    First met in: Block 10 · Figures in the plane · Concept

    Inscribed angle vertex on the circle #

    An angle with its vertex on a circle whose sides cut the circle.

    It equals half the central angle that stands on the same arc.

    First met in: Block 10 · Figures in the plane · Concept

    Property and test ⇒ and ⇐ #

    The two directions of a theorem: what follows from the kind of figure, and how to recognise that kind.

    The converse is not always true: a rectangle is not the only figure with equal diagonals.

    First met in: Block 10 · Figures in the plane · Concept

    Midline MN = AC/2 #

    The segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle or of the legs of a trapezium (US: trapezoid).

    The midline of a triangle is parallel to the third side and equals half of it; the midline of a trapezium is parallel to the bases and equals half their sum.

    First met in: Block 10 · Figures in the plane · Law

    Circumcentre (US: circumcenter) O #

    The point equidistant from all the vertices of a triangle: where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet.

    In a right triangle it is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, in an obtuse one a point outside the triangle.

    First met in: Block 10 · Figures in the plane · Law

    11 · Measurement in the plane #

    Cosine rule (US: law of cosines) c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C #

    Pythagoras' theorem for any triangle, corrected for the angle.

    For a right angle the cosine is zero, and the formula becomes Pythagoras' theorem.

    First met in: Block 11 · Measurement in the plane · Main idea

    Scale factor k #

    The number of times the lengths of one figure exceed the corresponding lengths of a similar one.

    Areas are in the ratio k², volumes in the ratio k³.

    First met in: Block 11 · Measurement in the plane · Concept

    Tangential quadrilateral a + c = b + d #

    A quadrilateral all of whose sides touch one circle.

    The sums of its opposite sides are equal, because each is made of the same tangent segments.

    First met in: Block 11 · Measurement in the plane · Law

    12 · Coordinates and vectors #

    Vector AB with an arrow #

    A directed segment; its coordinates show the shift along each axis.

    The coordinates of a vector are end minus start.

    First met in: Block 12 · Coordinates and vectors · Concept

    Collinear vectors a ∥ b #

    Vectors that lie on parallel lines or on one line.

    Their coordinates are proportional.

    First met in: Block 12 · Coordinates and vectors · Concept

    Scalar product a · b #

    A number: the product of the lengths of two vectors and the cosine of the angle between them.

    It equals zero if and only if the vectors are perpendicular.

    First met in: Block 12 · Coordinates and vectors · Concept

    Abscissa x in A(x; y) #

    The first coordinate of a point: its projection on the Ox axis.

    In the notation A(x; y) the abscissa comes first, and the Ox axis is called the axis of abscissas. On the unit circle the abscissa of the point of an angle is the cosine.

    First met in: Block 12 · Coordinates and vectors · Concept

    Ordinate y in A(x; y) #

    The second coordinate of a point: its projection on the Oy axis.

    In the notation A(x; y) the ordinate comes second, and the Oy axis is the axis of ordinates. A graph crosses the Oy axis at the point with abscissa 0, and its ordinate is the value of the function at zero. On the unit circle the ordinate of the point of an angle is the sine.

    First met in: Block 12 · Coordinates and vectors · Concept

    13 · Space: lines, planes, solids #

    Skew lines neither meet nor are parallel #

    Lines that do not meet and do not lie in one plane.

    Such pairs exist only in space; in the plane two lines either meet or are parallel.

    First met in: Block 13 · Space: lines, planes, solids · Concept

    Apothem height of a side face #

    The height of a side face of a regular pyramid.

    It goes into the area of the lateral surface; the volume takes the height of the pyramid.

    First met in: Block 13 · Space: lines, planes, solids · Concept

    Lateral and total surface S lat, S tot #

    The lateral surface is all the faces except the bases; the total one includes the bases.

    Mixing them up is one of the most frequent ways to lose a point in solid geometry.

    First met in: Block 13 · Space: lines, planes, solids · Concept

    Slant height l #

    The segment that sweeps out the lateral surface of a cylinder or a cone as it rotates.

    The slant height of a cylinder equals its height; the slant height of a cone is the hypotenuse of the triangle with legs R and h, so l² = R² + h².

    First met in: Block 13 · Space: lines, planes, solids · Law
